newsitem.title: USA: Clinton tax plan for education, middle class.
newsitem.headline: Clinton tax plan for education, middle class.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton unveiled a proposed tax cut compromise with congressional Republicans on Monday that concedes a modest reduction in capital gains taxes and insists that child tax credits benefit working poor families.

The president said he is willing to work with Republican leaders in the House and Senate to reach agreement on a net $85 billion five-year tax cut that he can sign into law. And, a top Republican commenting on the president's plan said he expects differences can be worked out.
The House of Representatives and Senate each passed versions of the tax bill, and conference committees will start negotiations towards a final bill in July.

"We are committed to work with the Republicans and this is a good-faith effort to do that, incorporating both their ideas for capital gains and some other things as well," Clinton said in a brief statement from the White House lawn as he departed for Boston.

Later he promoted the tax bill at a fund-raiser in Boston. "We're not talking about a huge bill here. What we are talking about is a bill that is basically the dividend the American people have earned for bringing this economy back."

The head of the tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee said he did not agree with Clinton's proposals, particularly the idea that families who pay no income tax should receive a child tax credit, but expressed optimism on the tax talks.

"Putting some differences aside, the president deserves credit and praise for joining with Republicans in endorsing our approach to tax relief," Representative Bill Archer, a Texas Republican said. "I'm upbeat that we will successfully conference our bills so the president can sign them into law."

Clinton's plan lowers the tax on investments, provides a phased-in $500-per-child tax credit calculated in such a way as to permit low-income parents to benefit, and includes $35 billion worth of tax breaks for higher education. He also offered a new, separate plan to increase the cigarette tax by 20 cents per pack with the proceeds to help children's health and other programmes. The Senate had passed a similar version.

Clinton also proposed to allow parents to save up to $1,000 per child in tax-free accounts for their child's education, a child's first home or for their own retirement. While the House and Senate bills contain elements of these, Clinton criticised them as skewed toward providing a larger share of benefits for higher-income people.
"They do an inadequate job of opening the doors to college ... They direct far too little relief to the middle class. They include time-bomb tax cuts that threaten to explode the deficit," he said.

The tax cut is a politically important part of the budget agreement worked out with Congress that aims to reduce the government's budget deficit to zero by 2002. Cutting taxes takes revenue from the government, but both sides have called it a "dividend" for the public.

Central to his plan is nearly $35 billion in tax cuts designed to encourage higher education. It was modified to give a maximum $1,500 tax credit in 1998 and a 20 percent tuition tax credit for the third and fourth years of college and would not be available for the wealthy. Clinton dropped the requirement that students maintain a "B" grade average.

The most costly tax break, worth $70 billion in five years, is the plan to give lower- and middle-income families with children under age 17 a $400-per-child credit next year. The tax credit would rise to $500 per child in 1999 and in 2003 children up to age 19 would be eligible. It would be partially refundable to those who pay little or no taxes.

On a cut in the capital gains tax rate paid on investment profits, the cornerstone of the Republican tax plans, Clinton offered an alternative that would allow exclusion from tax of 30 percent of the profits on investments from assets such as stocks, bonds and real estate held a year or more.

This would give a slight tax break to those in the top tax bracket -- a reduction in the tax rate to 27.7 percent from the current 28 percent, but would provide greater benefit to those with low and moderate incomes. The Republican bills cut the top capital gains rate to 20 percent from 28 percent.
Clinton continued to oppose the Republican plan to index the capital gains tax rate as a way to allow investors to escape tax on gains due to inflation.
